verses.zh: 我们既然蒙怜悯，受了这职分，就不丧胆，
verses.en: Therefore, since we have this ministry, just as God has shown us mercy,[NOTE:1] we do not become discouraged.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “just as we have been shown mercy”; ἠλεήθημεν (ēleēthēmen) has been translated as a “divine passive” which is a circumlocution for God as the active agent. For clarity this was converted to an active construction with God as subject in the translation.
verses.commentary:
4:1 "we" It is obvious that Paul is using the PLURAL PRONOUN to refer to himself, as he does
throughout this chapter. Grammarians called this "the editorial we."

▣ "we have this ministry" Paul is referring to "the ministry of the Spirit" (cf. 2 Cor. 3:8), also
called "the ministry of righteousness" (cf. 2 Cor. 3:9). Paul uses this word for service, diakonia,
so often in 2 Corinthians.

- diakonēo, 2 Cor. 3:3; 8:19,20

- diakonia, 2 Cor. 3:7,8,9; 4:1; 5:18; 6:3; 8:4; 9:1,12,13; 11:8

- diakonos, 2 Cor. 3:6; 6:4; 11:15,23

Christians are saved to serve (cf. Eph. 2:10). Christianity is not a "what's in it for me" focus
as much as "what can I do for others because of what Christ has done for me" focus. Paul served and called
all believers to service (cf. Gal. 2:20).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SERVANT LEADERSHIP

▣ "as we received mercy" God's mercy for Saul, who was such a staunch, militant, anti-Christian
(cf. 1 Tim. 1:13,16), on the road to Damascus (AORIST PASSIVE INDICATIVE, cf. Acts 9:1-22;
22:3-16; 26:9-18; 1 Cor. 7:25) encouraged him to continue to preach the Good News in the face of adversity and unbelief.

Paul wrote in Greek, but thought in Hebrew. The Greek term eleeō (i.e., mercy, pity,
compassion) is used in the Septuagint to translate the Hebrew term hesed (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS),
which relates to covenant fidelity. YHWH is faithful to His covenant promises, even when humanity is not (i.e., unconditional
covenants)! Paul's dramatic conversion clearly reveals the compassion of God. He acts in mercy to Jews (cf. Rom. 9:15,16,18,23-24; 11:30)
and to Gentiles (cf. Rom. 11:32) for His own covenant purpose, which is the restoration of His image in mankind
through the work of Christ and the ministry of the Spirit. God's loyalty to His covenant and His unchanging
character of mercy is mankind's only hope.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "we do not lose heart" This is PRESENT ACTIVE INDICATIVE. This must be understood in the
light of Paul's overall ministry and this particular context (cf. 2 Cor. 4:16). Paul did feel like giving up several
times. Jesus appeared to him in visions several times to encourage him (cf. Acts 18:9-10; 23:11; 2 Tim. 4:17, or an angel, Acts 27:24).
In this particular context, in the face of physical trials and problems with the church at Corinth, Paul had confidence
that the merciful, covenantal God was there and in control (cf. 2 Cor. 3:12). The task was too important to lose heart
(i.e., the Great Commission, cf. Matt. 28:19-20; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8).

verses.zh: 乃将那些暗昧可耻的事弃绝了；不行诡诈，不谬讲　神的道理，只将真理表明出来，好在　神面前把自己荐与各人的良心。
verses.en: But we have rejected[NOTE:1] shameful hidden deeds,[NOTE:2] not behaving[NOTE:3] with deceptiveness[NOTE:4] or distorting the word of God, but by open proclamation of the truth we commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience before God.
notes: L&N 13.156; the word can also mean “to assert opposition to,” thus here “we have denounced” (L&N 33.220).
Grk “the hidden things [deeds] of shame”; here αἰσχύνης (aischunēs) has been translated as an attributive genitive.
Or “not conducting ourselves”; Grk “not walking” (a common NT idiom for conduct, way of life, or behavior).
verses.commentary:
4:2 "we have renounced" This is AORIST MIDDLE INDICATIVE. There is a series of things which
Paul personally refused to use in his own ministry.

- no underhanded means

- no disgraceful methods

- no cunning

- no tampering with or watering down God's message

Each of these reflects the false teachers' charges or their actions.

NASB
"the things hidden because of shame"

NKJV, Peshitta
"the hidden things of shame"

NRSV
"the shameful things that one hides"

TEV
"secret and shameful deeds"

NJB
"shameful secrecy"

Paul uses similar phrases to describe slavery to sin in Rom. 6:21 (also note Eph. 5:1-12) and sins of
humanity which will be revealed in 1 Cor. 4:5 (also see 1 Cor. 14:25). In this context the phrase seems to describe
the methodology of the itinerant false teachers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHAME

NASB, NKJV
"not walking in craftiness"

NRSV, Peshitta
"we refuse to practice cunning"

TEV
"we do not act with deceit"

NJB
"it is not our way to be devious"

"Walking" is a PRESENT ACTIVE PARTICIPLE referring to the false teachers' lives
and tricky methods (cf. Eph. 4:14). Paul uses the term "crafty"
(i.e., "all" plus "work") several times in his letters to Corinth (cf. 1 Cor. 3:19; 2 Cor. 4:2; 11:3; 12:16).

We must be very careful about our methods as well as our goals. For in Christianity the means determine
the end. This same word, "crafty," is used by Paul

- in a quote from Job 5:13 referring to human wisdom (cf. 1 Cor. 3:19)

- of Satan tempting Eve (cf. 2 Cor. 11:3)

- of the trickery of Satan and the false teachers (cf. Eph. 4:14)

- here, of the methods of false teachers

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

NASB
"or adulterating the word of God"

NKJV, Peshitta
"nor handling the word of God deceitfully"

NRSV
"to falsify God's word"

TEV
"nor do we falsify the word of God"

NJB
"or to falsify the word of God"

This term and its related forms mean

- watered down (cf. 2 Cor. 2:17)

- entrapped with bait (cf. Matt. 26:4; Mark 14:1)

- defrauded or deceived (cf. 2 Cor. 11:13; Rom. 3:13)

It refers to a changing message based on the hearer's sensibilities or trying to trick the hearers (cf. 1 Cor. 1:23).
Paul did alter his presentation and illustrations depending on the audience, but never, never the gospel message.

NASB, NKJV, Peshitta
"by the manifestation of truth"

NRSV
"by the open statement of the truth"

TEV
"in full light of truth"

NJB
"by showing the truth openly"

For "manifestation" see full note at 2 Cor. 2:14.

The term "truth" has the ARTICLE and refers to the gospel of Christ, the New
Covenant. The false teachers acted in shameful ways, secret ways, but Paul preached the full truth publicly.

SPECIAL TOPIC: "TRUTH" IN PAUL'S WRITINGS

▣ "commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God" Paul is referring to his self-limiting
love for others (cf. 1 Cor. 9:19-23). This does not speak of compromise, but voluntary self-limiting of freedom because
of the cultural hang-ups or personal preferences of others. His intentionality was evangelism, not personal freedom
(cf. Rom. 14:1-15:13; 1 Cor. 8; 10:23ff; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRISTIAN FREEDOM vs. CHRISTIAN RESPONSIBILITY).

Paul uses these same terms in 2 Cor. 5:11-21, which also emphasize the gospel and our part in its
proclamation. See fuller note on "commend" at 2 Cor. 3:1.

See fuller note on "conscience" at 1 Cor. 8:7 and 10:25.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSCIENCE

▣ "in the sight of God" This seems to be an idiomatic phrase parallel to "God is my witness." Other
Pauline texts also use this phrase in a similar way (cf. Gal. 1:20; 1 Tim. 5:21; 6:13; 2 Tim. 2:14; 4:1), see full list of
Paul's oath taking at 2 Cor. 1:23; 11:31.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE DEITY

verses.zh: 如果我们的福音蒙蔽，就是蒙蔽在灭亡的人身上。
verses.en: But even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled only to those who are perishing,
verses.commentary:
4:3 "if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE, which is assumed to be true or
for the literary purpose of the author. Some people just do not get it (cf. Matthew 13).

▣ "our gospel is veiled" This is a PERIPHRASTIC PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE of "veiled"
(cf. 2 Cor. 3:14,16). It is obvious to Paul that when he preached the gospel some men absolutely could not respond to it.

- as the Jews are "hardened" (cf. Rom. 11:25; 2 Cor. 3:14; and Deut. 29:4; Isa. 6:9-10; 29:10)

- hearers in every age are also "blinded" (cf. 2 Cor. 4:4)

- this is the mystery of predestination versus free will, the paradox of the gospel (cf. John 1:12; 3:16 vs. 6:44,65)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELECTION

▣ "those who are perishing" Paul is continuing his analogy of the gospel as an aroma of life
and of death (cf. 2 Cor. 2:15; 1 Cor. 1:18-19; 8:11; 10:9-10; 15:18). The proclamation of the gospel is
serious business, to some life, but to some death.

For the concept of "perishing" see a discussion at 1 Cor. 1:18.

I have recently become aware of some very interesting biblical and historical studies of the
varied interpretations of "Hell" in the early church fathers, as well as texts such as this that mention "perishing" (i.e., John 3:16).
Please look at the following two YouTube videos with an oepn mind and an open Bible!

- Edward Fudge, The Fire That Consumes: A Biblical and Historical Study of Hell
YouTube One Hour Lecture

- Steve Gregg, Hell &#8210 Three Christian Views
YouTube Lecture
- 1:34:57

verses.zh: 此等不信之人被这世界的神弄瞎了心眼，不叫基督荣耀福音的光照着他们。基督本是　神的像。
verses.en: among whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of those who do not believe[NOTE:1] so they would not see the light of the glorious gospel[NOTE:2] of Christ,[NOTE:3] who is the image of God.
notes: Grk “the gospel of the glory”; δόξης (doxēs) has been translated as an attributive genitive.
Or “so that the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ would not be evident to them” (L&N 28.37).
verses.commentary:
4:4 "the god of this world" This evil personality is called by several names by Paul.

- Satan (cf. Rom. 16:20; 1 Cor. 5:5; 7:5; 2 Cor. 2:11; 11:14; 12:7; 1 Thess. 2:18; 2 Thess. 2:9; 1 Tim. 1:20; 5:15; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: SATAN)

- Devil (cf. Eph. 4:27; 6:11-12; 1 Tim. 3:6,7; 2 Tim. 2:26; the PLURAL used of the demonic,
1 Cor. 10:20-21; 1 Tim. 4:1; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: DEVIL)

- "the prince of the power of the air" (cf. Eph. 2:2)

- "the god of this age/world" (John calls him "the ruler of this age/world," John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11)

- "the tempter" (cf. 1 Thess. 3:5)

- "the evil one" (cf. 2 Thess. 3:3, this title is common in Matthew's and John's writings)

- "an angel of light" (cf. 2 Cor. 11:14)

This verse caused great concern to the early Church Fathers because it seemed to add fuel to the
fire of the Gnostic and Arian false teachers. Therefore, unfortunately, they (Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen,
Chrysostom, Ambrose, Theodoret, and Augustine) changed the Greek of this text to: "in who God has blinded
the mind of the unbeliever of this world." Now Satan is obviously referred to as the prince and power of
this world (cf. John 12:31; 14:30; Eph. 2:2). These early Church Fathers were not reacting to the concept
of a personal force of evil, but to the theological concept of the Gnostic Demiurge and the Arians' view of
a less-than-divine Christ.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSONAL EVIL

SPECIAL TOPIC: GNOSTICISM

▣ "of this world" This is also the Greek term for "age" (i.e., aiōnos) This
seems to refer to the Jewish view of two ages: the current evil age dominated by sin and the age to come,
set up and dominated by the Messiah (cf. Matt. 28:20; Eph. 2:2).

The terms "this world" (kosmos houtos) and "this age" (aiōn houtos) are
used interchangeably (cf. George E. Ladd's A Theology of the New Testament, p. 223).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THIS AGE AND THE AGE TO COME

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S USE OF KOSMOS (world)

▣ "has blinded the minds of the unbelieving" This is an AORIST ACTIVE INDICATIVE. The term is
used of spiritual blindness in Matt. 15:14; 23:16; 1 John 2:11 and the same concept is in John 9. This same term is
used in a quote from the Septuagint of Isa. 6:10 in John 12:40. It is a rather rare term in Paul's writings
(cf. Rom. 2:19 and here), but common in the Gospels.

In the Isaiah passage (i.e., Isa. 6:9-10) it is God's judgment that blinded the Israelites' spiritual
eyes because of their continual unbelief. This same truth is expressed in Rom. 1:21, where the PASSIVE VOICE
implies God (cf. Rom. 11:8-10, quoting Isa. 29:10 and Ps. 69:22-23). It is difficult to balance

- human unbelief

- divine hardening

- satanic blinding

Belief is a gift and a necessary response! The covenantal paradox is the mystery of predestination
and free will. We must let God be God and demand human accountability.

Can you imagine the power that the evil one must have that he is able to blind the eyes of
humans to the compelling beauty of the gospel (cf. Matt. 13:19) and the wooing of the Holy Spirit to respond
to it (cf. John 6:44, 65)? Paul uses several images to describe unbelief:

- hardened hearts

- blinded minds

- seared consciences

- blinded eyes

There is an ongoing spiritual conflict (cf. Eph. 2:2; 4:14; 6:10-19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD HARDENED

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRITUAL WARFARE

NASB
"so that they might not see the light of the gospel

of the glory of Christ"

NKJV, Peshitta
"lest the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ. . .

should shine on them"

NRSV
"to keep them from seeing the light of the

gospel of the glory of Christ"

TEV
"He keeps them from seeing the light shining on them, the light that

comes from the Good News about the glory of Christ"

NJB
"so that they cannot see shining the light of the gospel

of the glory of Christ"

If you will notice in this context, there are several words that relate to light. This refers to

- Jesus, often called "light" (cf. John 1:4,9; 3:19; 8:12)

- possibly Paul's experience on the Damascus road (cf. Acts 9)

- possibly an allusion to the Shekinah glory of God from the Exodus mentioned in 2 Cor. 4:6; 3:7); see
SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH

To not see Christ in the Scriptures is to miss salvation. The NT proclaims the glory of Christ, the
gospel. The OT is fulfilled and completed in Him (cf. Matt. 5:17-48; 1 John 5:10-12). He is the necessary foundation, cornerstone,
cap stone, top stone. To miss Him is to shipwreck one's faith.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS IS GREATER THAN

▣ "who is the image of God" See full note on "image" at 2 Cor. 3:18. To see Jesus is to see the Father (cf. John 1:18;
14:8,9; Col. 1:15; Heb. 1:3). The NT asserts that Jesus was incarnated to serve three purposes.

- to fully reveal the Father

- to atone for sin

- to give believers an example to follow

verses.zh: 我们原不是传自己，乃是传基督耶稣为主，并且自己因耶稣作你们的仆人。
verses.en: For we do not proclaim[NOTE:1] ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your slaves[NOTE:2] for Jesus’ sake.
notes: Traditionally, “servants.” Though δοῦλος (doulos) is normally translated “servant,” the word does not bear the connotation of a free individual serving another. BDAG notes that “‘servant’ for ‘slave’ is largely confined to Biblical transl. and early American times…in normal usage at the present time the two words are carefully distinguished” (BDAG 260 s.v.). One good translation is “bondservant” (sometimes found in the ASV for δοῦλος) in that it often indicates one who sells himself into slavery to another. But as this is archaic, few today understand its force. Also, many slaves in the Roman world became slaves through Rome’s subjugation of conquered nations, kidnapping, or by being born into slave households.
verses.commentary:
4:5 "we do not preach ourselves" Trying to interpret Paul's letter is like listening to only half
of a phone conversation. We assume from Paul's statements the things that might have caused them. From 2 Cor. 3:1,
here, and chapters 10-13, it is obvious that Paul had those at Corinth in mind who attacked him personally and his
gospel. Paul is forcefully asserting Jesus' Lordship and his servanthood (cf. 1 Cor. 3:5-9). He only defends
himself (i.e., "ourselves" is emphatic) or magnifies his credentials (cf. chapter 12) in order to protect
the validity of the gospel he preached. For an interesting discussion on the limits of apostolic authority see George
Ladd's A Theology of the New Testament, p. 382.

▣ "Christ Jesus as Lord" This phrase was the early church's profession of faith at baptism
(cf. Rom. 10:9-13; 1 Cor. 12:3; Phil. 2:9-11). All three of the major terms used in the NT to designate
the Promised One, the Suffering Servant, are used in this phrase.

- Christ ‒ This is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew term messiah, which meant "an anointed one." It
implies "one called and equipped by God for a specific task." In the OT three groups of leaders: priests,
kings, and prophets were anointed. Jesus fulfills all three of these anointed offices (cf. Heb. 1:2-3; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: ANOINTING IN THE BIBLE).

- Jesus ‒ This Hebrew name meant "YHWH saves" or "YHWH brings salvation." It was revealed to his parents
by an angel (cf. Matt. 1:21). "Jesus" is derived from the Hebrew word for salvation, hosea,
suffixed to the covenant name for God, "YHWH." It is the same as the Hebrew name for Joshua. See
SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

- Lord ‒ The term "lord" (kurios) can be used in a general sense or in a specific theological
sense. It can mean "mister," "sir," "master," "owner," "husband," or "the full God-man." The OT
usage of this term (adon) came from the Jews' reluctance to pronounce the covenant name
for God, YHWH, which was from the Hebrew VERB "to be" (cf. Exod. 3:14). They were
afraid of breaking the commandment which said, "Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God
in vain" (cf. Exod. 20:7; Deut. 5:11). They thought if they did not pronounce it, they could not
take it in vain. So, they substituted the Hebrew word, Adonai, which had a similar meaning
to the Greek word, Kurios (Lord; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord [adon and kurios]). The NT Authors used this term to describe the full deity of Christ.

There are several confessional phrases used of Jesus.

- Jesus is the Messiah/Christ ‒ Acts 5:42; 9:22; 17:3; 18:5,28; 1 Cor. 1:23

- Jesus is the Son of God ‒ Acts 9:20; Rom. 1:3-4; Heb. 4:14; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF GOD

- Jesus is Lord ‒ Acts 2:36; 10:36; 11:20; Rom. 10:9; 2 Cor. 4:5; Phil. 2:11; Col. 2:6

In a sense these summarize the early church's understanding of Jesus of Nazareth.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA OF THE EARLY CHURCH

▣ "and ourselves as your bond-servants for Jesus' sake" Paul saw himself as a "bond slave" to Jesus.
This is OT imagery for a Hebrew who freely chose to serve a master for life. Paul's life was not his own. His will
was not his own. He was tasked to serve Jesus' church.

verses.zh: 那吩咐光从黑暗里照出来的　神，已经照在我们心里，叫我们得知　神荣耀的光显在耶稣基督的面上。
verses.en: For God, who said “Let light shine out of darkness,”[NOTE:1] is the one who shined in our hearts to give us the light of the glorious knowledge[NOTE:2] of God in the face of Christ.[NOTE:3]
notes: An allusion to Gen 1:3; see also Isa 9:2.
Grk “the light of the knowledge of the glory”; δόξης (doxēs) has been translated as an attributive genitive.

‡ Most witnesses, including several early and significant ones (P46 א C H Ψ 0209 1739c M sy), read ᾿Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ (Iēsou Christou, “Jesus Christ”), while other significant witnesses, especially of the Western text (D F G 0243 630 1739* 1881 lat Ambst), have Χριστοῦ ᾿Ιησοῦ. The reading with just Χριστοῦ is found in A B 33 sa Tert Or Ath Chr. Even though the witnesses for the shorter reading are not numerous, they are weighty. And in light of the natural scribal proclivity to fill out the text, particularly with reference to divine names, as well as the discrepancy among the witnesses as to the order of the names, the simple reading Χριστοῦ seems to be the best candidate for authenticity. NA28 reads ᾿Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ with ᾿Ιησοῦ in brackets, indicating doubts as to its authenticity.
verses.commentary:
4:6 "For God who said, 'Light shall shine out of darkness'" This is an allusion to Gen. 1:3 (or possibly Isa. 9:2)
and a personal allusion to Paul's Damascus road experience (cf. Acts 9:1-22; 22:3-16; 26:9-18). For Peter the same kind of
revelatory experience involving Jesus and light (i.e., glory) occurred on the Mount of Transfiguration (cf. 2 Pet. 1:19).

▣ "hearts" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEART

▣ "glory of God" This seems to relate to the Shekinah cloud of glory that symbolized the presence
of YHWH in the book of Exodus (cf. 2 Cor. 3:17). This symbol of God's presence was transferred to the Ark of the
Covenant after the crossing of the Jordan River into the Promised Land. YHWH is fully known, not as a visible, physical
object, but in Jesus, the incarnation of Deity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (OT)

▣ "in the face of Christ" This is the continuing comparison between the veil of Moses
(cf. 2 Cor. 3:13) and the perfect reflection of Jesus Christ (cf. John 1:18; Heb. 1:3). Believers see the
glory of Christ in His life, death, resurrection, and teachings. Jesus is the full and final revelation of
the God of Israel, the Creator (cf. 2 Cor. 3:18).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL

verses.zh: 我们有这宝贝放在瓦器里，要显明这莫大的能力是出于　神，不是出于我们。
verses.en: But we have this treasure in clay jars, so that the extraordinary power[NOTE:1] belongs to God and does not come from us.
notes: Grk “the surpassingness of the power”; δυνάμεως (dunameōs) has been translated as an attributed genitive (“extraordinary power”).
verses.commentary:
4:7 "But we have this treasure" This refers to God's indwelling Spirit that magnifies, reveals, and
forms the person of Christ in our lives (cf. John 16:8-14; Rom. 8:9; Col. 1:27; 2 Pet. 1:3-4).

▣ "in earthen vessels" This is an emphasis on the human body (cf. 2 Cor. 4:10,16; 5:1ff;
Gen. 2:7; 3:19; 18:27). This entire context is a dialectic between Paul's physical earthly condition
and the tremendous spiritual power of the gospel and the indwelling Holy Spirit in his life.

Paul speaks of his current physical body in several ways in this context.

- "earthly vessel" ‒ 4:7

- "outer man" ‒ 4:16

- "earthly tent" ‒ 5:1

- "natural body" ‒ 1 Cor. 15:44,46

- "a living soul" ‒ 1 Cor. 15:45

- "from the earth, earthly" (i.e., "made of dust") ‒ 1 Cor. 15:47

- possibly, "the old man" ‒ Col 3:10

▣ "the surpassing greatness" Huperbolē, see

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S USE OF HUPER COMPOUNDS

verses.zh: 我们四面受敌，却不被困住；心里作难，却不至失望；
verses.en: We are experiencing trouble on every side,[NOTE:1] but are not crushed; we are perplexed,[NOTE:2] but not driven to despair;
notes: Grk “we are hard pressed [by crowds] on every side.”
verses.commentary:
4:8-11 "we are afflicted in every way, but not crushed" Verses 8-10 contain a series of nine PRESENTS
(mostly PASSIVE PARTICIPLES) which are word plays on Koine Greek words describing Paul's difficult
ministry. The first eight PARTICIPLES are in contrasting pairs. The first term describes Paul's ministry
experience and the second term limits the consequences. Examples of this word play are:

- "at loss but not utter loss"

- "knocked down but not knocked out"

This section can be compared to 2 Cor. 1:6; 6:4-10; 11:23-28.

verses.zh: 遭逼迫，却不被丢弃；打倒了，却不至死亡。
verses.en: we are persecuted, but not abandoned;[NOTE:1] we are knocked down,[NOTE:2] but not destroyed,
notes: Or “badly hurt.” It is possible to interpret καταβαλλόμενοι (kataballomenoi) here as “badly hurt”: “[we are] badly hurt, but not destroyed” (L&N 20.21).
verses.commentary:
4:9 "destroyed" The term translated "destroyed" by NASB means "to desert," "abandon," or "forsake." It implies
that even amidst terrible circumstances the believer is never left alone! Believers will face persecution but never
abandonment! The veil was removed from Paul's mind and now he fully recognized the Triune God's presence with him.

verses.zh: 身上常带着耶稣的死，使耶稣的生也显明在我们身上。
verses.en: always carrying around in our body the death of Jesus,[NOTE:1] so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible[NOTE:2] in our body.
notes: The first clause of 2 Cor 4:10 is elliptical and apparently refers to the fact that Paul was constantly in danger of dying in the same way Jesus died (by violence at least). According to L&N 23.99 it could be translated, “at all times we live in the constant threat of being killed as Jesus was.”
verses.commentary:
4:10 "always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus" This refers to the paradox of our being
rightly related to God, but exposed to physical problems because of the three enemies of mankind (i.e., the world, the flesh, and
the Devil, cf. Eph. 2:2-3). We have eternal life, but we are physically dying (cf. 2 Cor. 1:8). As Jesus was rejected and persecuted
(cf. John 15:20), so too, are believers (cf. 1 Cor. 15:31; Gal. 2:20; Phil. 3:10; Col. 1:24; 1 Pet. 4:12-19).

▣ "so that the life of Jesus" This refers to

- the resurrected Christ, which was Paul's hope

- the faithfulness of Jesus under persecution

Paul wanted to exhibit Jesus' faithfulness (cf. 2 Cor. 4:11) and participate in the resurrection
of His followers (cf. 2 Cor. 4:14; 1 Cor. 15).

▣ "may be manifested in our body" This is an AORIST PASSIVE SUBJUNCTIVE. Read
Gal. 6:17, which obviously refers to Paul's physical scars in Jesus' service. As our earthly vessel is
broken, the treasure inside is more visible (cf. 2 Cor. 12:9-10).

Paul uses the Greek term sarx (i.e., flesh) in several senses.

- the human body ("body" of 2 Cor. 4:10 parallel to "flesh" of 2 Cor. 4:11; also 2 Cor. 7:5; 10:3; 12:7)

- human person (cf. 2 Cor. 5:16; 11:18)

- human descent (i.e., father - son, cf. Rom. 1:3; 4:1)

- humanity as a whole (cf. 1 Cor. 1:26,29)

- human sinfulness (cf. Rom. 7:5,18; 8:3,4,5,8,9,12,13; 2 Cor. 7:1; 10:2)

SPECIAL TOPIC: FLESH (sarx)

verses.zh: 因为我们这活着的人是常为耶稣被交于死地，使耶稣的生在我们这必死的身上显明出来。
verses.en: For we who are alive are constantly being handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible[NOTE:1] in our mortal body.[NOTE:2]
verses.commentary:
4:11 "we who live are constantly being delivered over to death for Jesus' sake" Theological insight
into this verse can be seen in 1 Cor. 4:9, where the Apostles are on exhibition both to angels and men.
Believers also are on exhibition to a lost world as well as the angelic world (cf. Eph. 2:7; 3:10).

The term "constantly" (cf. 2 Cor. 6:10) is parallel to "always" of 2 Cor. 4:10. The call
to ministry is a call to intentional daily death to self (cf. 2 Cor. 5:14-15; Rom. 6:7; 1 Cor. 15:31;
Gal. 2:20; Phil. 3:8,10; 1 John 3:16). This attitude is the reversal of the fall of mankind in Genesis 3.
It is evidence of the believer's transformation into Christlikeness, which is the restoration of the image of God in humanity.

The term "been delivered over" (paranididōmi) was used

- of Judas handing over Jesus to the authorities (cf. Matt. 20:18-19; Mark. 10:33)

- by Jesus in a prophetic sense describing His followers in Matt. 10:17; 24:9; Mark 13:11-12

The phrase "for Jesus' sake" is to be understood as causality. Our ministry burdens do not
benefit Christ, but they are ours because we follow Him. As they persecuted Him, they will persecute us (cf. Rom. 8:17).
However, it is also true that the things we suffer as Christ's followers are the very things that can help
us grow more and more like Him.

Paul's identification with Jesus' death functions theologically on several levels.

- sacramental theology (cf. Rom. 6:3-5; Col. 2:12; 3:1,3-5)

- church doctrine (cf. 1 Thess. 4:14-15)

- personal experience (cf. 2 Cor. 4:10-11; Gal. 2:20; Phil. 3:10)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY DO CHRISTIANS SUFFER?

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRISTIAN GROWTH

▣ "mortal flesh" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: FLESH (sarx)

verses.zh: 这样看来，死是在我们身上发动，生却在你们身上发动。
verses.en: As a result,[NOTE:1] death is at work in us, but life is at work in you.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “death is at work in us, but life in you”; the phrase “is at work in” is repeated in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
4:12 "So death works in us, but life in you" This is a PRESENT MIDDLE (deponent) INDICATIVE
which personifies death. This refers to physical persecution for Paul and his mission team (cf. 2 Cor. 4:16) and
spiritual life in them who have responded to his presentation of the gospel.

In The Anchor Bible series on 2 Corinthians Victor Furnish believes it is PASSIVE VOICE (p. 257)
because that VOICE dominates 2 Cor. 4:10-11, where the understood subject is the power of God
(cf. 2 Cor. 4:7). This would imply that God uses trials and persecutions as a means of producing Christlikeness
in His followers (as it did in Jesus, cf. Heb. 5:8). Leaders' lives give power to their messages (cf. 2 Cor. 1:3-11; 2 Tim. 2:9-10).

verses.zh: 但我们既有信心，正如经上记着说：「我因信，所以如此说话。」我们也信，所以也说话。
verses.en: But since we have the same spirit of faith as that shown in[NOTE:1] what has been written, “I believed; therefore I spoke,”[NOTE:2] we also believe, therefore we also speak.
verses.commentary:
4:13 "having the same spirit of faith" The significant thing here is that the same "faith" that made
a person right with God in the OT (i.e., the writer of Psalm 116) is the faith that makes a person right
with God in the NT (i.e., Abraham in Gen. 15:6, quoted by Paul in Rom. 4:3,9,22).

Paul is using the term "spirit" in the sense of a person's self. He often uses "spirit" as a
way of referring to the inner qualities of a human person (see note at 2 Cor. 4:21). This is
not related to the similar phrase found in 1 Cor. 12:9, which refers to the
Spirit gifting believers with faith. This refers to saving faith such as Abraham's (cf. Gen. 15:6).
Interestingly, in Word Studies in the New Testament, vol. 2, M. R. Vincent says, "not distinctly
the Holy Spirit, nor, on the other hand, a human faculty or disposition, but blending both; faith as a
gift of the Spirit of God" (p. 82).

In Synonyms of the Old Testament, Robert Girdlestone has an interesting discussion
of the uses of the term "spirit" in the NT (pp. 61-63).

- evil spirits

- the human spirit

- the Holy Spirit

- things that the Spirit produces in and through human spirits

- 'not a spirit of slavery vs. a spirit of adoption' ‒ Rom. 8:15

- 'a spirit of gentleness' ‒ 1 Cor. 4:21

- 'a spirit of faith' ‒ 2 Cor. 4:13

- 'a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him' ‒ Eph. 1:17

- 'not a spirit of timidity vs. power, love and discipline' ‒ 2 Tim. 1:7

- 'spirit of error' vs. 'spirit of truth' ‒ 1 John 4:6

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE NT

▣ "according to what is written" This is a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE,
which was a Hebrew idiom used by OT authors to refer to the givenness and relevance of Scripture (cf. Matt. 5:17-19).

▣ "I BELIEVED, THEREFORE, I SPOKE" This is a quote from the
Septuagint of Psalm 116:10, which speaks of God's rescue of a saint.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

verses.zh: 自己知道那叫主耶稣复活的，也必叫我们与耶稣一同复活，并且叫我们与你们一同站在他面前。
verses.en: We do so[NOTE:1] because we know that the one who raised up Jesus[NOTE:2] will also raise us up with Jesus and will bring us with you into his presence.
notes: Grk “speak, because.” A new sentence was started here in the translation, with the words “We do so” supplied to preserve the connection with the preceding statement.

‡ Several significant witnesses (א C D F G Ψ 1881), as well as the Byzantine text, add κύριον (kurion) here, changing the reading to “the Lord Jesus.” Although the external evidence in favor of the shorter reading is slim, the witnesses are significant, early, and diverse (P46 B [0243 33] 629 [630] 1175* [1739] r sa). Very likely scribes with pietistic motives added the word κύριον, as they were prone to do, thus compounding this title for the Lord.
verses.commentary:
4:14 "that He who raised the Lord Jesus" This phrase is an excellent opportunity to show that the
NT often attributes the works of redemption to all three persons of the Godhead.

- God the Father raised Jesus (cf. Acts 2:24; 3:15; 4:10; 5:30; 10:40; 13:30,33,34,37; 17:31;
Rom. 6:4,9; 10:9; 1 Cor. 6:14; 2 Cor. 4:14; Gal. 1:1; Eph. 1:20; Col. 2:12; 1 Thess. 1:10)

- God the Son raised Himself (cf. John 2:19-22; 10:17-18)

- God the Spirit raised Jesus (cf. Rom. 8:11)

There are several variants related to the phrase, "the Lord Jesus."

- "the Lord Jesus" ‒ MSS א, C, D, F, G

- "the Lord Jesus Christ" ‒ MS 436

- "the Lord Jesus from the dead" ‒ MSS 104, 459

- "Jesus" ‒ MSS P46, B

The UBS4 gives option #1 a "B" rating (almost certain), but Bruce Metzger prefers
option #4 (as does the NET Bible). As with so many of the variants, which one was original does not
affect the overall thrust of the passage. A book that has helped me deal with the textual variants in Scripture is
The Lost World of Scripture, by John Walton and Brent Sandy, which discusses how oral cultures pass
on their traditions!

SPECIAL TOPIC: RESURRECTION

▣ "will raise us. . .will present us" These are both FUTURE ACTIVE INDICATIVES. Believers
will be raised from the dead (PREPOSITION sun with Jesus) and presented to the Father
(sun with all believers).

Paul's understanding as to the time of the Second Coming is ambiguous.

- in some texts it seems that he expected to be alive at the parousia (cf. 1 Thess. 4:15,17; 1 Cor. 15:51-52; and Phil. 3:20; 4:5)

- in other texts he seems to identify himself with those believers who have died (cf. 1 Cor. 6:14; 2 Cor. 4:14; 5:1-10)

Only the Father knows the time of the Second Coming (cf. Matt. 24:36; Mark 13:32; Acts 1:7). The Second
Coming is the hope of every generation of believers, but the reality of only one generation. Believers are to
live ready, ready by being active in Christ's service.

verses.zh: 凡事都是为你们，好叫恩惠因人多越发加增，感谢格外显多，以致荣耀归与　神。
verses.en: For all these things are for your sake, so that the grace that is including[NOTE:1] more and more people may cause thanksgiving to increase[NOTE:2] to the glory of God.
verses.commentary:
4:15 Paul's heart was to help sinful people

- come to faith in Christ

- find true peace and joy

- give God praise (cf. 2 Cor. 1:11 and NASB, NRSV, TEV, NJB)

The NKJV is a bit more literal "to the majority."
This may refer to Paul's supporters in the Corinthian church. It would be opposite of the "some"
(cf. 2 Cor. 3:1; 10:12; 1 Cor. 4:18; 6:11; 8:7; 10:7,8,9,10; 15:6,12,34,35). Verse 15 is obviously
a doxological summary.

▣ "the glory of God" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (OT)

verses.zh: 所以，我们不丧胆。外体虽然毁坏，内心却一天新似一天。
verses.en: Therefore we do not despair,[NOTE:1] but even if our physical body[NOTE:2] is wearing away, our inner person[NOTE:3] is being renewed day by day.
verses.commentary:
4:16 "Therefore we do not lose heart" This is a recurrent theme in Paul's writings (cf. 2 Cor. 4:1; Gal. 6:9;
Eph. 3:13; 2 Thess. 3:13). Difficult circumstances are, in reality, for strengthening our spiritual stamina and fruitfulness.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY DO CHRISTIANS SUFFER?

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRISTIAN GROWTH

▣ "but though our outer man is decaying, yet our inner man is being renewed day by day" These are both
PRESENT PASSIVE INDICATIVES, which denote ongoing action. The PASSIVE VOICE is hard to
translate and understand in this context. Most English translations translate them as ACTIVE VOICE, but
they also may denote divine action in using physical problems and persecutions as a means to strengthen and mature
Jesus' followers (cf. Matt. 5:10-12; John 15:18-21; 16:1-2; 17:14; Acts 14:22; Rom. 5:3-4; 8:17; 2 Cor. 4:16-18;
Phil. 1:29; 3:11; 1 Thess. 3:3; 2 Tim. 3:12; Heb. 5:8; James 1:2-4; 1 Pet. 4:12-19).

In Eph. 3:16 and 4:24 there is a comparison of the old man and the new man, but the contrast
here is between our outer physical body and our inner spiritual nature.

▣ "is being renewed" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: RENEW (anakainōsis)

▣ "day by day" Paul uses Hebrew idiomatic (cf. Gen. 39:10; Esther 3:4; Ps. 68:19) repetition in
2 Cor. 4:16, "day by day," and a similar Hebraic repetition in 2 Cor. 4:17, "excessively to excess"
(i.e., huperbolēn eis huperbolēn). Remember, NT authors (except Luke) are Hebrew/Aramaic
thinkers writing in Koine Greek. There are many Hebraic idioms and grammatical constructions, as well as
numerous OT allusions and quotes in the NT. Also note that the proper definition of terms is not found in
contemporary Koine Greek literature, but in the Septuagint, which is the Greek translation of the OT.

verses.zh: 我们这至暂至轻的苦楚，要为我们成就极重无比、永远的荣耀。
verses.en: For our momentary, light suffering[NOTE:1] is producing for us an eternal weight of glory far beyond all comparison
verses.commentary:
4:17-18 Verse 17 is very similar to Rom. 8:18, while 2 Cor. 4:18 is similar to Rom. 8:24. Paul wrote
the book of Romans from Corinth! He had been thinking about his call and the problems connected to it. There was, in
reality, no comparison between the momentary light affliction and the eternal glory! This is the biblical
worldview that sustains God's people in this fallen world. He is with us, for us, and will bring us into His
personal presence to remain forever!

4:17 "is producing" This same VERB is used in Rom. 5:3-4 and James 1:2-4, which also
speaks of the benefits of suffering and persecution.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- How does 2 Cor. 4:1 speak of the methods of the false teachers?

- Were the early church fathers justified in changing the Greek text of 2 Cor. 4:4 to meet the problem of their day?

- Why is Paul drawing such attention to his physical problems versus his spiritual strengths?
